message.content:
**Earliest non‑Christian historical reference to Jesus Christ**

| Source | Date (approx.) | Passage | Why it matters |
|--------|----------------|---------|----------------|
| **Flavius Josephus – *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 18, Chapter 3** | 93–94 CE | “Now there was a wise man named **Jesus**… He was crucified by Pontius Pilate.” | Josephus was a first‑century Jewish historian writing for a Roman audience. His account is the earliest surviving mention of Jesus outside the New Testament, and it is generally considered authentic (the “Testimonium Flavianum” is widely accepted as containing a genuine core, though later Christian interpolations may have been added). |
| **Tacitus – *Annals*, Book 15, Chapter 44** | 116 CE | “The emperor Tiberius… ordered the execution of **Christ**, the founder of the name.” | Tacitus was a Roman senator and historian. His brief reference confirms that Jesus was executed under Pontius Pilate and that the movement survived into the early 2nd century. |
| **Pliny the Younger – *Letters*, 1.9** | 112 CE | “The Christians worship **Christ** as a god.” | Pliny’s letter to Emperor Trajan provides evidence that the cult of Christ existed in early 2nd‑century Rome. |
| **Babylonian Talmud – *Sanhedrin* 43a** | 3rd–5th century CE | “Jesus was hanged on the eve of Passover.” | A Jewish rabbinic source that corroborates the crucifixion narrative, though it is later than the Josephus and Tacitus accounts. |

### Bottom line
The **earliest surviving historical record** that mentions Jesus Christ outside the Christian scriptures is **Josephus’ *Antiquities of the Jews* (c. 93–94 CE)**. Subsequent references by Tacitus, Pliny, and the Talmud confirm and elaborate on the basic facts of his life and death, but they come after Josephus.
